summary: Describes how multiple signatures work in the Cryptographic Message Syntax. It adds ways to indicate relationships between signatures and to deal with concerns when a signer attaches more than one SignerInfo. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: If several people sign a paper, you may want to know which signatures belong together and in what order. This document adds a way to label that.

questions: how do multiple signatures work in cms
what is a signature downgrade attack
what is the cms multiple-signatures attribute
subtitle: A signed attribute that lets a verifier notice when someone strips the stronger of a signer's several CMS signatures.

tldr.problem: A signer may add several SignerInfo structures to a CMS SignedData, using different digest or signature algorithms. An attacker who broke the weak algorithm can delete the others, and the remaining signature still verifies.
tldr.mechanism: Each SignerInfo carries a signed multiple-signatures attribute with one value for every other SignerInfo from the same signer. Each value holds the algorithms and a hash of that other SignerInfo's signed attributes, so a missing one can be detected.
tldr.outcome: A relying party can tell that a SignerInfo was removed. The attribute does not help if every algorithm in use has been broken. The RFC also gives non-normative advice on combining multiple signature results.

facts.label: Values per SignerInfo
facts.value: Signatures by the signer, less one

today: RFC 5752 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2010. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
In the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS, RFC 5652), a SignerInfo carries what a relying party needs to verify a signer's digital signature. A signer puts more than one SignerInfo into a SignedData when using different digest or signature algorithms. Each exists independently, so SignerInfo structures can be added or removed without disturbing the others.

That independence is the concern. If an attacker has broken one hash or signature algorithm, they can remove every SignerInfo except the broken one. The relying party is left with the attacked signature even if it supports stronger algorithms. The fix is for signers to include a pointer to all of their own SignerInfo structures, so a removal becomes visible.

The attribute is not the countersignature attribute. A countersignature is a serial signature over an existing signature. The attribute here points to parallel signatures by the same signer at the same level.
sections.eli5: If you sign a paper in two ways, each signature also lists the other one. Then nobody can quietly tear one off.

sections.title: The Downgrade Problem
sections.content:
The rationale is protection against downgrade attacks that remove the strong signature and leave the weak one. Removing a SignerInfo does not make the signature invalid and is not an error, so the relying party may not even know a second one existed.

The RFC walks through a signer who produces a weak and a strong SignerInfo. A relying party that supports only the weak algorithm, or only the strong one, can verify what it supports and MAY consider the signature valid. A party supporting both can process both, and local policy may require both to validate. Local policy MAY also decide that removal of the strong signature makes the result invalid.

The attribute must use the CMS attribute structure, be computable before any signatures are applied, identify individual SignerInfo objects, and resist collision, preimage and second preimage attacks.
sections.eli5: Some people can read only the pencil signature, some only the pen one, some both. Someone who can read both should be able to tell if one has been rubbed out.

sections.title: The multiple-signatures Attribute
sections.content:
The multiple-signatures attribute points to the signer's other SignerInfo objects. With three signatures, each SignerInfo holds two attribute values: the 1st points to the 2nd and 3rd, the 2nd to the 1st and 3rd, and the 3rd to the 1st and 2nd. So a SignerInfo carries one value per signature by that signer, less one. The attribute MUST be a signed attribute and is multi-valued. It is identified by id-aa-multipleSignatures.

Each value is a MultipleSignatures structure:

  • bodyHashAlg: the digest algorithm of the referenced SignerInfo.
  • signAlg: the signature algorithm of the referenced SignerInfo.
  • signAttrsHash: an algID that MUST match the digest algorithm of the SignerInfo holding this value, and a hash of the referenced signedAttrs.
  • cert: optional. It identifies the certificate that signed the referenced SignerInfo, and MUST be present if the fields in the other multiple-signatures attributes are the same.
sections.eli5: Each signature carries a little list. Each entry says which other signature exists, how it was made, and a fingerprint of it.

sections.title: Generating and Verifying
sections.content:
Signers follow the CMS procedures with additions. The signer MUST retain existing signerInfo objects and include its own. The signer MUST include the multiple-signatures attribute in signedAttrs of each SignerInfo.

Because each hash covers signed attributes that themselves contain the attribute, the RFC gives an order. First, all other signed attributes are placed in each SignerInfo, with no signatures computed yet. Second, the multiple-signatures attributes are added with a zero-length octet string in SignAttrsHash.hash. Third, the correct hash is computed for each SignerInfo. Fourth, the hash values are placed into their fields.

To verify, the number of values in a SignerInfo MUST equal the number of that signer's SignerInfo objects less one. Each hash MUST match the result of the calculation above for the SignerInfo it points to.
sections.eli5: First write everything except the fingerprints. Then work out each fingerprint, and copy them into place at the end.

sections.title: Evaluating Several Signatures
sections.content:
This section is non-normative, but the processing is highly recommended. A message may have several SignerInfo objects in one SignedData, or several SignedData objects nested inside each other. The order is: evaluate each SignerInfo independently, combine results at the same level, then combine nested SignedData results.

A single SignerInfo is judged on three pieces: whether the signature mathematics succeeds, fails or cannot be evaluated; whether the source of the public key (usually a certificate) is valid, with outcomes Success, Failure, Indeterminate or Warning; and local and application policy about the contents.

By default, a set of SignerInfo objects is combined by grouping them by signer, taking the best result for each signer, then taking the worst result across signers. Policy can change every step. A workflow application might care only about the outermost signature, while a signed mail application might ignore failed outer signatures and show the inner valid one.
sections.eli5: Check each signature on its own. For one person who signed twice, the better result counts. Across different people, the worst result counts.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of the hash and signature algorithms used for the SignerInfo apply. If hashing and signing are done by different entities, the signing entity must make sure the hash comes from a trustworthy source. Requiring multiple hashes with different algorithms can partly mitigate this.

The attribute cannot be relied on if all algorithms used in it are cracked, because a verifier cannot tell that no collision satisfying all of them could be found. Local policy and application requirements also affect processing, so a signature valid in one context can fail in another.
sections.eli5: The trick only works if at least one of the ways of signing is still strong. If all of them are broken, nothing can be trusted.
